Conflict across Myanmar’s townships

January 2021–September 2025

Le Truong Chinh · ISSS626

2026-10-05

Conflict and continuing needs

Myanmar’s armed conflicts predate the February 2021 coup, after which fighting spread into more central areas. By December 2024, OCHA estimated that almost 3.5 million people were displaced within the country, with education and healthcare severely disrupted.

This study follows 53,805 events across 330 townships over 57 months, from January 2021 to September 2025. It covers battles, explosions/remote violence and violence against civilians.

I compare each township with its neighbours and follow changes month by month. Civilian targeting and reported deaths help identify places that incident totals alone could overlook.

I want to keep continuing needs in view: families may still need support after recorded fighting has eased, as well as where violence is increasing.

Methods: Local Moran’s I and Gi* for clusters; Mann–Kendall and EHSA for changes through time. Data: ACLED Myanmar, supplied through eLearn; MIMU v9.4. Conflict background.

The monthly total peaked in late 2023

The total reached 1,465 events in November 2023. January to September 2025 recorded 12.4% fewer events than the same months of 2024. Explosions and remote violence remained the largest category.

127 townships recorded increases

Kawkareik, Kyaukpyu and Nawnghkio had the largest rises. Rakhine’s total fell by 734, while Kyaukpyu added 207. Kyaukpyu’s neighbours averaged 53 fewer events, so the regional decline hides a local increase.

Maungdaw ranks higher for reported deaths

Maungdaw ranks 17th by incidents but third by reported deaths (1,583). Kale has the highest reported death toll (1,877). I would want local clinics and aid groups to help assess what affected households still need in both townships.

These are estimated deaths reported across the included conflict events, covering civilians and combatants.

Most hotspots are in central Myanmar

Gi* identifies 38 hotspots: 18 in Sagaing, seven in Mandalay and six in Magway.

Its 53 coldspots include 13 in Ayeyarwady, 11 in Yangon and ten in Shan (East).

Local Moran’s I places 38 townships in high-count clusters and 52 in low-count clusters. Four have low counts despite higher counts nearby.

Neighbours share an edge or corner. Hotspots and coldspots have unusually high or low neighbourhood counts (p < 0.05). Three island townships have no shared-boundary neighbours.

How hotspot patterns changed

EHSA finds 26 oscillating hotspots, which ended hot after earlier cold months, and eight sporadic hotspots, which were hot on and off without cold months.

The EHSA map shows the 23 hotspots and 42 coldspots that also pass the trend test. Kawkareik and Nawnghkio show rising concentrations.

Monywa was a hotspot throughout 2022 to 2024, but no longer met the threshold in September 2025. I would still want its ongoing needs checked before reducing aid.

Monthly results include neighbouring townships and the preceding month. The map shows significant trends only (p < 0.05).

New hotspots around Kawkareik

Hotspots fell from 27 to 18 between the matched periods. Five of the seven townships that became hotspots in 2025 border Kawkareik. Hlaingbwe rose from one to 41 events and still qualifies after a stricter check for chance findings.

Both maps use January to September and the same neighbours. They compare hotspot labels; the change between years has not been tested directly.

Little change in civilian targeting

16,391 events in the study targeted civilians.

Their map has 37 hotspots, with 34 overlapping the overall conflict hotspots.

Hakha, Tonzang and Nawnghkio appear only in the civilian-targeting hotspot map.

In January to September 2025, civilian-targeting events were only 2% lower than in the same months of 2024. In 26 townships, they rose while total events fell. This concerns me most when reading the national decline.

Counts refer to events where civilians were targeted and exclude incidental civilian harm. Tonzang has only two such events; its hotspot label mainly reflects nearby townships.

Stricter checks narrow the hotspot list

  • Allowing for chance findings across many tests reduces the overall hotspot count from 38 to 19.
  • Using the six nearest townships as neighbours keeps 87.2% of classifications unchanged among townships with shared-boundary neighbours.
  • Accounting for similarities between nearby months reduces significant trends from 218 to 148. 126 remain after also allowing for the number of tests.
  • Kawkareik and Nawnghkio still show rising concentrations after these checks.

Reporting coverage, approximate locations and township size affect the counts. The maps show recorded conflict; assessing current safety also needs local information.

Recommended actions

I would use these findings to start discussions with local aid groups about where support is still missing.

  • Check gaps in food, shelter and medical support in Sagaing, Mandalay and Magway, which contain 31 of the 38 hotspots.
  • Ask aid groups in Kawkareik, Kyaukpyu and Nawnghkio whether displacement has increased demand beyond their capacity. Include Hlaingbwe and Kawkareik’s other neighbours.
  • Contact clinics and aid groups in Kale and Maungdaw about household needs following the high reported death tolls.
  • Review displaced households’ housing, food and healthcare needs in Monywa before reducing existing aid.
  • Follow up on rising civilian targeting in Pakokku and Myaing. Check the incidents behind the civilian hotspots in Hakha, Tonzang and Nawnghkio, including nearby townships.

Update the records beyond September 2025 and confirm current needs with local aid groups before acting.

I would also like to compare nearby townships’ monthly changes and understand whether communities facing rising civilian targeting can reach clinics and aid.
